catalog_quote: XII. 4. Stress. Stress in Awankari is prominent. ... Stress is mostly a matter of intonation and will be discussed as such later. But here some broad features of the incidence of stress may be mentioned. XII. 4 i. Disyllabic words (1) When a long or half-long vowel occurs finally in both syllables, stress is even ... (2) When the two syllables are short, stress is again even. ... (3) When the first syllable is long and the second short, there is slight stress on the first ... (4) There is prominent stress on the final syllable when it is long, preceded by a short syllable, i'mán, faith ... o'gás, sky ... EXCEPTIONS. Variation in stress is due to expressiveness. Exception to No. (4) occurs in Past participles and a number of loanwords. ... Similarly exceptions to No. (2) occur in a number of abstract nouns and some verbal forms ... XII. 4 ii Trisyllabic words ... In Awankari, as a rule, …

(2) Deciding source: a descriptive phonetics monograph (published Ph.D. thesis) devoted to the Awankari dialect, with a dedicated stress section; Glottolog files Awankari (avan1234) under Southern Hindko and Shackle 1980, downloaded now, both confirms that dialect placement ('Hindko proper': Avankari, Ghebi, Attock, Kohat) and rates Bahri's volumes 'of outstanding quality'. sources.citation: Bahri, Hardev. 1962. Lahndi Phonology [with special reference to Awankari]. Allahabad: Bharati Press (Part II of the 1944 Punjab University thesis; historical phonology). archive.org item lahndi-phonology (scanned text)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Historical volume; says the Awankari stress system is simple and stress 'exceptionally strong' (Pakhri sub-dialect 'stress is very strong', causes consonant doubling), that Awankari 'has normally preserved Sanskrit stress-accent' with exceptions, and refers the synchronic description to Lahndi Phonetics and to its own accent chapter. Nothing that alters the penult / disyllable-by-length coding.
sources.locator: Introduction (dialect features (5)-(6)), sec. I.5 'Stress' (the scanned text)

sources.quote: Abbottabad = Northern Hindko [hno], not this languoid; only asserts Hindko is 'predominantly a syllable-timed language' with even prominence; no word-stress placement rule and no Southern Hindko data.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.quote: TOC only (body is behind De Gruyter paywall; publisher site returned a WAF challenge). Glottolog ref 568752 language note: 'Hindko-Abbotabad = Hindko-Northern [hno]' - the Hindko described is Northern, not Southern Hindko.
sources.locator: TOC: 3.4.1.3 Stress, 3.4.1.3.1 'Stress in Hindko' p. 49 (one page)
sources.note: Modern reference grammar with an explicit one-page Hindko stress section; describes Abbottabad (Northern Hindko [hno]) so it is comparative only, but it is the only recent linguist-authored stress statement for any Hindko variety and would show whether Bahri's penult/vowel-length pattern is pan-Hindko.

sources.citation: Shackle, Christopher. 1980. Hindko in Kohat and Peshawar. Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 43(3): 482-510. doi:10.1017/S0041977X00137401 (archive.org item hindko-in-kohat-and-peshawar, scanned text + text PDF)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: No word-stress placement rule stated; only incidental references to 'post-accentual closed syllables' (epenthetic -o- generalized there in Ko./Pe.) and 'accented diphthongs in monosyllables'. Confirms identity and authority: Avankari (Av.) is a member of 'Hindko proper' with Ghebi, Attock-Haripur and Kohat Hindko; Bahri's Lahndi Phonology (1962) and Lahndi Phonetics (1963) 'are studies of outstanding quality' and the LSI description 'has been completely superseded by the excellent material presented by Bahri'.
